note: SBA borrowing principle: borrow composition, concepts and ways of thinking about materials — never copy the style.

same: Both focus on people's isolation in city life
Both start from everyday spaces (restaurants, homes)
diff: Edward Hopper (霍普) uses realist oil painting and strong light and shadow; Pak Sheung-chuen (白雙全) uses conceptual art and ready-mades
Hopper depicts scenes; Pak measures and materialises space itself
sba: Borrow Hopper's window-frame / glass divisions in your composition to show the distance between people
Borrow Pak's concept of 'collecting invisible things' to turn the cramped pressure of subdivided flats and classrooms into visible objects

same: Both use natural scenery to carry inner states
The brushstrokes / ink marks themselves are traces of emotion
diff: Vincent van Gogh (梵高) uses high saturation and swirling impasto; Lui Shou-kwan (呂壽琨) uses blocks of dry, dark ink and blank space
Van Gogh's emotions burst outward; Lui leans towards Zen-like introspection
sba: Borrow Van Gogh's 'brushstroke direction expresses emotion', using line rhythm to record how your mood changes over a day
Borrow Lui's blank space to give the picture room to breathe, expressing calm or detachment

same: Both give up recognisable images and use colour to create a spiritual space
Both aim for an immersive emotional experience for the viewer
diff: Mark Rothko (羅斯科) uses large soft-edged colour blocks in a still structure; Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極) brings in calligraphic brush movement, so his pictures flow
Zao is rooted in Chinese landscape painting and calligraphy; Rothko comes from Western colour field painting
sba: Borrow Rothko's layered colour blocks, using two or three colours to express one emotion
Borrow Zao's brush movement, turning calligraphic gestures into an abstract composition

same: Both appropriate familiar popular images and commercial brands
Both use the visual language of mass production, such as flat colour and repetition
diff: Andy Warhol (沃荷) shows the surface of American consumer culture and celebrity worship
Wang Guangyi (王廣義) places political propaganda posters next to Western brands, with an ironic edge
sba: Borrow repeated arrangement (a screen-print effect) to explore the brands or social media images in students' daily lives
Borrow the idea of 'juxtaposing two image systems' to create critical meaning

same: Both explore identity through images of people
Both use symbolic objects to tell stories
diff: Frida Kahlo (卡蘿) uses self-portraits to confront bodily pain and Mexican culture
Wilson Shieh (石家豪) uses gongbi fine brushwork in rich colour and faceless figures to explore Hong Kong identity and gender roles
sba: Borrow Kahlo's 'self-portrait + symbolic objects', using things around you to express your own identity
Borrow Shieh's Chinese gongbi technique with contemporary subjects to create a dialogue between tradition and the present

same: Both break everyday logic to create a dreamlike feeling
Both have humour and poetry
diff: René Magritte (馬格利特) paints impossible scenes in a calm, realist manner
Luis Chan (陳福善) uses bright colours and naïve forms, with a sense of fantasy and folk humour
sba: Borrow Magritte's 'displacement', putting familiar objects into illogical scenes
Borrow Luis Chan's free use of colour to turn Hong Kong street scenes into a fantasy world

same: Both make the installation / experience of space the artwork itself
Both make viewers notice perceptions they usually overlook
diff: Olafur Eliasson (埃利亞松) uses natural phenomena such as light, water and mist, on a grand scale
Lee Kit (李傑) uses canvas, projection and everyday objects, with a quiet, intimate mood
sba: Borrow Eliasson's use of light to change how a space feels, and make a small light installation
Borrow the mood of Lee Kit's 'small everyday moments' to record your home space

same: Both explore close relationships through portraits / group portraits
Both deliberately flatten the picture
diff: David Hockney (霍克尼) uses bright colours to show life and friends in California
Zhang Xiaogang (張曉剛) uses grey tones and 'bloodline' threads to evoke collective memory and a sense of repression
sba: Borrow Hockney's double-portrait compositions to analyse distance and relationships between figures
Borrow Zhang Xiaogang's 'old photos + thin connecting lines' to show family memory

same: Both seek order and balance in the picture
Both use lines to divide space
diff: Piet Mondrian (蒙德里安) uses vertical and horizontal lines and primary colours: pure geometry
Wucius Wong (王無邪) combines design principles with Chinese landscape, so geometry and ink coexist
sba: Borrow Mondrian's grid divisions to show city planning or a timetable
Borrow Wucius Wong's way of placing design elements in landscape to create an East–West fusion composition

same: Both explore states of existence through sculptures of the human body
Both use 'missing' parts to spark the imagination
diff: Alberto Giacometti (賈柯梅蒂) stretches and thins the body to express existentialist loneliness
Bruno Catalano (卡塔拉諾) hollows out the body to express the loss felt by travellers and migrants
sba: Borrow Giacometti's exaggerated proportions to express a psychological state
Borrow Catalano's 'missing parts' to express diaspora or things lost while growing up
